text:
2012
Compact nuclear power had long been considered intractable for civilian use. But on a cold December day, at an alternative energy conference, a team of academics reveals a new discovery: charging up small nuclear reactors over several days at high energy can produce clean power output. It is not yet competitive with other energy sources, but it does seem promising. The name of this new technology is Compact Nuclear Power (CNP).
Some note that at larger energy loads, CNP cores might become unstable, leading to meltdowns or explosions. The risks remain theoretical for now.
OpenAtom
Fuel materials and CNP core design continue to improve. ExxonMobil releases some early commercially viable cores. It is becoming clear that this technology will be transformative—at minimum, it will accelerate world energy production at a time that it is greatly needed, and some even say that it will unlock transmutation, creating plentiful quantities of various elements from feedstock. A group of concerned nuclear engineers convene to create a nonprofit, OpenAtom, that will distribute the benefits of the technology better than a private company would.
Its stated goal: "Our goal is to advance energy distribution in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return... it’ll be important to have a leading research institution which can prioritize a good outcome for all over its own self-interest."
Given the competitive nature of what the technological race could develop into, OpenAtom commits to joining efforts of other humanity-focused nuclear energy producers in its charter, if it runs into a scenario where race dynamics would limit the capacity to develop CNP in a safe manner.
Notwithstanding, the same document maintains "OpenAtom must be on the cutting edge of nuclear energy development—policy and safety advocacy alone would be insufficient."
The concerns around the new technology are not universal. Leading nuclear physicist Arnold Ng adds, "Worrying about a massive CNP explosion today is like worrying about ChatGPT going rogue."
Concerns multiply
Social media is abuzz with reports that the big energy providers are mining uranium in large quantities. The environmental movement is enraged. Some critics say that the uranium depletion pales in comparison to existing coal mining and oil drilling, but their reports never quite seem to curb the uranium outrage.
2023
In May, CNES, the Center for Nuclear Energy Security, releases an open letter: "Mitigating the risk of planetary explosion should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and AI takeover." CEOs of the foremost nuclear energy companies and nuclear scientists sign.
That summer, OpenAtom releases a statement saying: “Currently, we don't have a solution for shielding or controlling a potentially supernuclear core, and preventing it from exploding.”
April 3rd, 2025
A nonprofit investigating the rate of progress on nuclear energy production, the Nuclear Futures Project, releases a scenario forecast where they predict that supernuclear energy production is possible—but with high odds of blowing up the entire planet. Vice President TJ Mantz remarks: "We could wake up very soon in a world where there is no protection from nuclear explosions."
Later in July, the US government unveils a directive: Winning the Race—America's Nuclear Action Plan. It calls for faster energy production and removal of regulations.
April 2026
Elemental announces a new core with improved power density. Rumors surface that the core can convert traces of certain long-lived radioactive isotopes into shorter-lived ones. The process still requires carefully prepared samples, but appears to work across a wider range of materials than earlier cores. Some researchers see it as an early sign that CNP could eventually produce scarce elements from common feedstock.
At the same time, Elemental finds that it can use these new cores to accelerate improvements in radioactive shielding. It spins up a program for other organizations to improve their ability to remove nuclear fallout, in case of any future CNP meltdowns.
Amarillo
It is July 16th. Residents on the outskirts of the Texas city of Amarillo are awakened in the early morning to a deep boom. Later, they learn that an OpenAtom CNP has exploded. The fallout kills thousands of livestock from local ranches, but thankfully, no people are killed. The ranches affected by the fallout sue for $100 million in damages.
OpenAtom lets a group of three researchers enter its facilities and examine some security footage. The initial records are incomplete, and the investigation’s scope excludes earlier incidents. OpenAtom subsequently provides more footage. The researchers produce a report describing a network of over a thousand linked cores, hundreds of which were involved in the chain reaction.
Sept 2026
OpenAtom releases a result: using some of its ultra-high-energy cores, it is able to convert lead into silicon. The new cores are still unavailable to the government or wider public.
The world hears, some for the first time, that the employees at nuclear energy companies are increasingly worried about the technology. One writes:
I resigned from Elemental today. I spent the last three years doing thermal physics research at both OpenAtom and Elemental. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to build supernuclear machines and gambling with our lives. More thoughts below.
A researcher currently at Elemental adds:
He's correct here—we really do earnestly believe CNPs could trigger a world-destroying explosion! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Elemental is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve spontaneous reactor blowups and are not clearly on track to.
Less than a week later, Elemental's CEO publishes an essay titled Nuclear Caution. In it, he prescribes the need to slow the acceleration of energy production and high-energy experiments. OpenAtom, DeepCore, and xNuke CEOs join him in supporting the need for nuclear energy companies to slow the rate at which they accelerate energy production.
In the aftermath of these indictments, news reporters find themselves asking the nuclear researchers the same question: "How would CNPs actually explode?" The response: "We don't understand the mechanisms of how CNPs could actually produce as much energy as they are. It's hard to predict how they could actually explode, there are so many ways it could happen that would be unimaginable from our vantage."
CNP explosions become so routine that the month of October is christened "Grey October". However, Elemental and OpenAtom continue with their programs to help rural communities with the fallout cleanup.
Nov. 5, 2026
NETR, the Nuclear Evaluation and Threat Research nonprofit, releases a report of Elemental’s progress on CNP development. It estimates that the pace of improvements on standardized core-performance tests has roughly doubled relative to the earlier trend. The evaluators tentatively attribute most of the acceleration—perhaps 80%—to using existing cores in the development of better ones, with substantial uncertainty.
The full report is not available to the public. Company leaders shelve a project looking to investigate the energy allocation used on CNP development. The report that is released is full of redactions—Elemental’s RSO (Responsible Scaling Officer) maintains that further knowledge of the lab’s processes would enable competitors to produce more and more energy, making it possible to create cores that could be more dangerous than those made before. The extent to which Elemental's leadership is willing to slow down its own efforts remains unclear.

title: Catastrophic Talent Misallocation
excerpt: The central talent problem in AI safety is not “making the number of full-time people in AI safety go up” but “supporting niche talent needs”. It is becoming clearer what work lies on the critical path, and the majority of people in AI safe
text:
The central talent problem in AI safety is not “making the number of full-time people in AI safety go up” but “supporting niche talent needs”. It is becoming clearer what work lies on the critical path, and the majority of people in AI safety are not doing it.
Rationale:
1. The situation is urgent. Note that this is not necessarily the same as timelines being short, but it is similar. The political winds are shifting (perhaps in our favor) while AI becomes a partisan issue and labs are getting closer to RSI.[1]
2. There is a massive misbalance in the number of people working in certain subfields relative to their importance. The number of aligned people working in comms is probably in the double digits. There is at least 10x that amount of people working on technical research, and I don’t think that comms is less than 10% as important as technical research. Of course, not all of the technical researchers would be great at comms, but I find it hard to believe that less than 10% of them would be decent, especially if put on the right team.
3. We don’t need safety engineers at labs papering over cracks.[2] However, the fact that they have crack-papering experience is valuable in speaking credibly about the risks, whether to DC people or mass audiences.
4. I suspect that many current employees of METR or Redwood are smart enough that they could tackle a new vertical (e.g. operationalizing what a kill switch looks like) relatively soon, but I find it harder to believe someone new to AI safety could do the same successfully, because they lack connections and general AI risk know-how.
5. The first comms and generalist fellowships (mostly) happened this year. There have been over 10 iterations of MATS, which has churned out great results, but there are a ton more MATS alumni than Generator alumni.
Counterarguments:
1. It’s good to not put all your eggs in one basket. My counter-counterargument is that even if all the fieldbuilding orgs decided tomorrow to spend twice as much time on talent allocation as capacity building, I still would not expect us to overcorrect within the next 6 months.
2. There are new streams of talent available to us that weren’t there pre-Coxon/HF, and we should take advantage of that. I agree with this, although I don’t see enough people working on this either.
3. It’s easier to hill-climb on “# of people in AI safety”, and really make your pipelines efficient. Building a lot of ad-hoc transfer pipelines takes time.
Weak version of my argument: Even if you disagree with the above, I don’t think it’s a stretch to say that fieldbuilding orgs should make large changes to their prioritization. I think it’s rather clear that getting a single person who has 10+ years of DC experience and connections into the field would be a couple OOMs more impactful than a junior technical researcher.
^See METR’s report today: since October 2025, benchmark scores for Anthropic’s internal models have grown at about twice their historical rate (1.9x, 95% CI 1.5–2.8x).
^Note I’m not arguing that we need 0, just less on the margin.

title: Talk to people at happy hours
excerpt:
All too often we (at least myself) deliberate over which high-hanging fruit to pluck, when there’s low-hanging fruit right in front of us. Talking with more people at happy hours is a low-hanging fruit.
[1]
If you’re newer to AI safety and
text:
All too often we (at least myself) deliberate over which high-hanging fruit to pluck, when there’s low-hanging fruit right in front of us. Talking with more people at happy hours is a low-hanging fruit.
[1]
If you’re newer to AI safety and are invited to a happy hour, you should talk with more people outside your social circle at happy hours.
Much of the most recent strategic thinking in this space isn’t written down, and if it is, it’s in private Slack channels. Events are where the private Slack channels turn semipublic. You’re able to tap into insights that are otherwise expensive to get outside (email fancy person, hope they read your message) or from your unknown unknowns (you’ve already grokked the takes of people in your milieu).
You can laser in on relevant information when conversing to a greater degree than skimming through someone’s writing. Consider each individual’s mind to correspond to a library of experiences. Skimming their LessWrong is like browsing some of the shelves.
[2]
Talking face-to-face is like chatting with the librarian that knows the catalogue and can recommend you to resources (although in many cases they don’t need to, because they can summarize the exact content).
If you’re in SF/Berkeley, it’s likely that you’ve become desensitized to the fortune you have to be there. It might be motivating to reflect on what you would do earlier on in your AI safety journey if you had the chance to attend these events.
When you strip away the familiarity we have with many AIS professionals by virtue of the efforts they make to be available, you come up with a list that newbies to other industries would kill to meet their equivalents of. Here are people that I talked to today
[3]
:
The AI safety YouTuber who made the first AI safety content I ever saw/read
CEO of the org that founded the world’s largest AI safety space and pioneered one of the major research directions in technical AIS
Grantmakers who move more per year than I could earn in dozens of lifetimes
CEO of the OG AI safety org
Researcher at one of the handful of labs building superintelligence, which on the default path will succeed within 5-10 years
Most of these facts are in the “well, duh” category. My point with adding these is to get you to take a step back and notice, not to make some claim that these are the most important details or the most important people to talk to. In fact, some of the most valuable conversations were with others who had similar context levels to me and we could work through a crux together.
By this point, I hope you’re seeing the value in the thesis here. But what if you’re anxious about this whole thing? A few recommendations:
Go over to the event in a group and chat with your friends beforehand. This helps you warm up and discuss the things that really are more fun to talk about with those you already have rapport with.
Find a group of 5+ people and hang around the edges. No one will care if you come or go.
For any group where the participants are outward-facing or there’s a gap, it’s fair play to just walk up and start listening in. There are two outcomes: 1) The group notices, they introduce themselves, and you’re off to the races; or 2) The group continues chatting, you get to listen in, and they don’t mind your presence.
Identify a major question you have about your project and someone who has moderate background on the area you’re working in. People are normally happy to spitball on things they have some knowledge of, and you can choose topics that you naturally have a lot of experience in.
Consider that you don’t have to suddenly gain all the courage you’ll need. Value your decisions by the end world they lead to, not the immediate one. Even if you just gain 10% more confidence each happy hour, after about 7 times you will have doubled your confidence.
Something that has held me back earlier is that I feel like I’m detracting from more senior people’s experience at these events.
It might very well be the case that you are detracting from their experience! But in the long run, you will sooner get to the point where you are actively contributing to strategic discussion, putting you on the path to more effectively reducing x-risk.
Consider the case where someone brand new to AI safety strikes up a conversation with you and is curious and attentive. My guess is that you will enjoy this conversation.
More established people have had more reps than you politely making moves to exit conversations, and in my experience you don’t need to worry much about them holding a silent grudge over an unproductive conversation.
Naturally, this advice only applies if you’re lucky enough to have invites to these events and live in The Bay, DC, or London. This is worth a separate post, but attending conferences like EAGs, participating in courses or fellowships, or knowing alumni of AI safety programs is normally enough to get on the list, whence it’s easier to meet people who can invite you to more, etc. ↩︎
One could argue that with a good algorithm, this is more like browsing the “top picks” shelf. ↩︎
I wrote this a while ago and am only just publishing this, so technically not today anymore. ↩︎

title: Lateral Workshop Applications: A Case Study
excerpt:
We’re running a three-day program for experienced professionals moving into AI safety. See our announcement post for more details.
Lateral Workshop received over 700 applications for its first cohort. We were happily surprised by the range
text:
We’re running a three-day program for experienced professionals moving into AI safety. See our announcement post for more details.
Lateral Workshop received over 700 applications for its first cohort. We were happily surprised by the range and quality of experiences, and decided to expand the workshop to accept more applicants. Inevitably, the majority of applications were rejected, and I (Jacob) wanted to put down some notes for people considering next steps.
First off, there were some top candidates who we wanted to accept but didn’t have capacity for. We agonized over a few that we saw promise in but had to prioritize participants who we thought that we could provide more value to. In addition, we fully admit that our review can never be perfect, despite involving domain experts throughout the process. There are surely a handful of people who were rejected not because of their background but because we misread their presentation of it throughout their application responses and resume.
I’ll focus on the most tractable fixes to common patterns we saw. Applicants who portrayed clear competency in their career stood out, but it’s possible to make up for a lack of experience with deep thoughtfulness and working on building your field-level understanding.
Understand the priorities of the AI safety field. We decided to interview nearly all of the applicants who articulated field priorities cleanly. There are certain concerns that fall within what the ecosystem is presently built to support; many valid risks are better suited to work in adjacent fields. Good places to start include LessWrong, the 80,000 Hours podcast, or AI Futures Project’s scenarios.
Look into neglected risks. Current risks typically have a greater mass of corporate and governmental energy dedicated to them, whereas future risks are often neglected even in cases where early solutions are tractable. Learn how to reason about risks in a scope-sensitive manner.
But be authentic. There were applicants who gave us answers that felt like they were trying to guess at the “correct” answers. Ultimately we care about your thoughtfulness, not that you memorized the correct language to use.
Gain knowledge of AI safety organizations and their research directions or policy proposals. Normally this type of information is hard to glean from websites; reading a few reports authored by researchers at the organization or their personal Substack or LessWrong posts is a step in the right direction.
Include any costly signals of commitment to a career transition and clear-eyed thinking around next steps. If applicants put together a Saturday reading group or took time off work for self study, we want to know! We also appreciate people who had thought through how Lateral in particular would help them reach their goals, as opposed to other existing fellowships.
If asked to discuss your strengths, don’t spend too long rehashing your resume. People sometimes don’t realize that the skills important to a small, mission-driven field are quite distinct from the skills that got them to their current role. Curious and open-minded responses here fare well.
Write in your own voice. LLM-produced applications consistently underperformed (LLM usage was discouraged but not banned). The issue with LLM-generated text is that it makes you sound the same as everyone else, not only in tone but also reasoning style. Low quality applications can be improved marginally, but they are still so far below the bar that this doesn’t matter. Higher quality applications that would have had a chance to pass on to an interview are pushed down towards the mean, and increase the risk that reviewers miss your insights.
Ensure your resume is well formatted. Despite my best efforts to look past the format, when readability suffers, it makes it harder to advance the applicant.
Stay away from fluffy language. Transparent reasoning was rated higher. Clear explanations of the causal chain for the risks applicants care about fared better than gesturing in a broad direction.
Out of these points, the lion’s share of the misses were from people who hadn’t internalized the priorities of the field. My guess for why this is the case is that one learns this through diffusion, by parsing a variety of sources, although I don’t think that it would take an inordinate amount of time. See Matt Beard’s post for a clear roadmap.
Here’s a list of resources to look at if you haven’t considered them:
Global Challenges Project November Workshop: three-day workshop in London for professionals; applications due October 2.
Successif, SteadRise, High Impact Professionals, 80,000 Hours, and Probably Good offer free, virtual career advising.
ControlConf and FAR.AI events: various events on subfields of (mostly technical) AI safety.
EAG New York: large convening event for AI safety and other high-impact cause areas; applications due September 27.
Impact Accelerator Program: six-week virtual program for experienced professionals transitioning into high-impact careers.
BlueDot Incubator Week: weeklong program for founders looking to start something in AI safety.
Horizon Institute: workshops, events, career accelerators, and advising for those interested in AI policy.
AI Security Bootcamp: weeklong intensives for security professionals looking to secure frontier AI systems.
SPAR: part-time remote research program with technical, governance, security, and biosecurity projects; applications due August 18. (Express your interest to get notified about future cohorts afterwards.)
ML4Good, ARENA, and CAMBRIA: bootcamps for rapid upskilling in technical AI safety or AI governance.
BlueDot Career Transition Grants: grants to help financially sustain exploration, learning, and job searches as you transition into AI safety.
Thank you to Dillon Nguyen, Spencer Kitts, James Lester, and Eliana Du for feedback on a draft of this post.

title: What Mormons get right about community building
excerpt: Mormons get a lot of things right. Apart from strange Masonic temple rituals, they lead rather normal—and even excellent—lives. Mormons enjoy a longer lifespan,[1] Utah is the #1 state for volunteering,[2] and their language training progra
text:
Mormons get a lot of things right. Apart from strange Masonic temple rituals, they lead rather normal—and even excellent—lives. Mormons enjoy a longer lifespan,[1] Utah is the #1 state for volunteering,[2] and their language training programs are so successful that missionaries are a known source for foreign service and intelligence careers.
Throughout this post, I'll be making generalizations of Mormons rather than hedging the claims properly. I grew up in Wisconsin, Maryland, and Utah, and many of the claims are more true of the Utah/Idaho/Arizona corridor (affectionately called the "Morridor" by some ex-Mormons) than the rest of the US, and certainly the rest of the world.
Religions share much in common with AI safety and other impact-driven movements, and even more so the Mormon church. There are a few reasons for this:
Commitment to the cause. Anecdotally, nearly all of the ~500 Utah Mormons I've interacted with have been true believers, and only a handful just went to church out of habit.[3]
High stakes. Mormons do believe (I've heard they are trying to disavow this, but it was taught) that they will get a planet or some portion of the cosmos as their own if they are good in this life, and become Gods of their own. This is not far off from many transhumanist utopic visions. However, it's also true that they believe that before God's Second Coming, the world will go into a state of war and disarray, not unlike the forecasts of extinction-level risks bearing fruit.
Urgency to attract new members. Given the stakes, it's not a hard followup to believe that you should do what you can to teach more people about the awesome[4] benefits and risks awaiting them. Talent-constrained movements feel a similar urgency that is a little more impact-focused than community-focused.
Insularness. It's hard to be friends with someone outside the church, since being a member is a significant social and time commitment, and most people (in Utah) you interact with are members anyway. This contributes to both a sense of community and lack of viewpoint diversity.
Building community is a first-order priority
Mormons' focus on fostering community enables them to be effective at all the non-religious stuff they do.
Geography
First, some background: wards are composed of perhaps 50 to 100 families. There's no shopping around for congregations—ward membership is determined by where you live. This facilitates getting to know people. Each Sunday, the whole ward gets together for services, which are sometimes followed up by potlucks. Wednesdays, the kids get together for activities. Saturdays are for a rotating schedule of cleaning the church. Throughout the week, families are often close enough together that they see each other frequently.
Ministering
Within a ward, families are assigned a pair of people that minister to them: visit them once a month to check in, and maybe go over a spiritual lesson. While in the worst case these feel contrived, oftentimes people feel like they can count on their ministers to support them. With a few rotations of these over the years, you begin to develop a network of people that you wouldn't have naturally become friends with. This parallels the adage of "you get most job opportunities from acquaintances, not close friends": creating connections from across the network helps everyone to be fewer degrees away from each other.
Trek
Every four summers, the youth of the ward recreate the Mormon pioneers' crossing of the plains. In true 1800s fashion, they pull handcarts. A particularly exciting phase of this when I went involved the "Womens' Pull", where only the girls pulled and pushed the handcarts. (I think this was to simulate the number of men who died during the crossing). Afterwards we learned how to square dance. The only inauthentic aspect was how delicious the food was; we weren't served gruel. As my grandmother has often stated, "They didn't have McDonald's back then", and this increased our shared gratitude. Most of all, it increased our friendship.
Callings
Adult ward members are assigned callings, which range from choir director to primary instructor (children's religion classes) to bishop (equivalent of a pastor or imam). Callings aren't application-based, and a former bishop might be called to run nursery, the Sunday activities for toddlers. This flattens the hierarchical structures that would otherwise arise. Additionally, switching positions over the years helps each ward member feel connected to others, no matter their skills or interests that would normally push them to certain roles in the workforce.
Fast offerings
On the first Sunday of every month, Mormons hold a 24-hour fast from eating and drinking, aside from the sacramental rituals of eating a gob of (normally white) bread and a thimbleful of water. Aside from making the Sunday dinner delicious, Mormons save fast offerings, payments meant to cover the expenses of what they would have paid on food. Young men go door to door, collecting these payments (this is increasingly not the case; when I was doing it at 14, many people paid online. But they did give me amazing frozen Hershey's almond bars, which they made us promise not to eat until after breaking our fasts). The offerings go to the Bishop's Storehouse, where the money is converted into food for the hungry. The only other thing I heard about that place was that they had the best chocolate milk.
Being ingroupy allows you to move faster
When there is a shared value framework, people develop trust quicker. Upon moving into a new ward, a Mormon family will immediately have a community of like-minded people who do similar activities to them. Since they don't have to figure out whether they have to watch their tongues while discussing their morals, they can put more energy into getting to work and learning more about the people around them.
This also enables Mormons to dedicate more time resolving the surface-level issues, rather than revisiting foundational differences when interacting with others.
Do I think it's worth it to increase the ingroupy-ness of mission-driven movements? Not necessarily. Viewpoint diversity matters a lot more when the answers aren't legislated. Ingroupy-ness also limits the number of people who can join the movement.
Implications
Here are a few ideas vaguely inspired by Mormonism:
Create a platform for facilitating virtual 1-1s, especially between people from distinct backgrounds or positions
Create a travel grants program, so that people can benefit from geographic proximity
Instead of e.g. donating 10% of your income, precommit to donating a 24-hour period of your time each month to helping other people
Overall, I think we could do well by taking cues from other movements that have succeeded—in one way or another—at building community.
^Probably due to the frequency they attend religious services; similar effects have been observed for other religious adherents. A 2004 Utah study finds that, compared to non-LDS people, there is a 7.3-year difference in life expectancy for males and a 5.8-year difference for females.
^https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2023/01/volunteering-and-civic-life-in-america.html
^This leaves out the people who were PIMO: physically in, mentally out. However, amongst those people, I've found that they developed a strong belief that the church was not true, so the same principle holds.
^In the biblical sense

title: Announcing Lateral Workshop for experienced professionals moving into AI safety
excerpt: TL;DR: Lateral Workshop is a program in Berkeley from September 11–13 for mid-career and senior professionals who are interested in transitioning into AI safety work to meet people in the field and explore how they can fit in. If you have e
text:
TL;DR: Lateral Workshop is a program in Berkeley from September 11–13 for mid-career and senior professionals who are interested in transitioning into AI safety work to meet people in the field and explore how they can fit in. If you have experience in another field and are interested in translating that experience into impact in AI safety, apply here by August 9th!
If AI safety is to keep scaling, we’ll need a lot of people that the field currently doesn’t supply well. People who know how to run 30+ person organizations. People who have deep connections in DC. People with specialized knowledge in cybersecurity or verification.
Professionals from outside AI safety have those skills, but it’s been difficult for them to make the switch. The professionals we have spoken with rarely lack relevant skills. More often, they struggle to understand how the field works, where they could contribute, and how to become credible candidates. Here are some of the specific barriers experienced professionals face while trying to transition:
Difficulty in understanding the key priorities of the field
Lack of networks within the field and poor understanding of where to start to build them
Lack of free time to invest in time-intensive upskilling and context building
Financial risk (getting a role is competitive, and the field is insular enough that rejections from roles are correlated)
Difficulty evaluating a young and unfamiliar field that lacks many of the conventional markers of professional maturity
Some professionals do navigate these barriers through persistent self study and deep attempts to understand the field. But requiring every candidate to independently reconstruct the field is slow and unnecessarily costly. AI safety has reduced similar friction for students by building clearer early-career pipelines; we think experienced professionals could benefit from a similar investment in talent pipelines and infrastructure.
Even after some contact with the field, it has been hard to hire experienced professionals:
In virtually all cases, the reason organizations must hire experienced talent in the first place is because the role has higher stakes. A good leader can make an organization go well, while a poor leader can devastate culture and sink an organization quickly.
Organizations are currently hesitant to take bets on people. This may be a good policy for individual organizations to follow, but can simultaneously be negative on the ecosystem level.
Hiring rounds index heavily on in-group signals that are correlated, but not necessarily causal to impact. These disadvantage people who come to AI safety from outside the main cultural context.
Professionals are sometimes poorly calibrated on which of their skills are useful—many of their specialized technical skills are less applicable to AI safety, but the tacit people-modeling knowledge they have is applicable.
Here are some excerpts from example roles requiring experienced talent:
“7–8+ years of senior communications experience … building or owning crisis communications frameworks, with an understanding of reputational risk management” – Head of Communications & PR, Apollo Research
“You’re a strong engineer with solid infra fundamentals. You can dig into unfamiliar systems, debug from logs, and identify and fix performance bottlenecks” – Member of Technical Staff, Evaluation Execution, METR
“Multiple years of relevant research or policy experience and a track record of producing high-quality work” – Research Fellow, GovAI
“Closer to 10 years [of experience] for a COO profile.” – Chief Operating Officer, Encode
“Own initiative areas end-to-end — from recruiting founders and designing organizations to commissioning products and running fellowships” – Principal, Project Development, Future of Life Foundation
“Write a coalition letter and get twenty organizations to sign it, ranging from religious groups to workers' rights advocates” – Policy Advisor, Encode
Pipeline legibility
A research-oriented person has a relatively defined ladder: BlueDot → ARENA → SPAR → MATS → junior researcher → senior researcher. For mid-career non-research talent, the paths look like this:
Founder: BlueDot → Catalyze or another incubator → hopefully get funding
Operations person: BlueDot → get hired, somehow
Generalist: BlueDot → do unspecified things for a year → Generator
There's a missing intermediate step between introductory content and the programs that place people. For professionals, there are few clear steps after a BlueDot course.
It’s not just about content learning: for early-career people, university groups provide the grounds to transmit context, culture, and motivation, and there's nothing similar for professionals. Successful mid-career transitions have happened by individuals who have forged their own paths, because nothing existed for them.
Past solutions
Workshops are able to significantly affect the career paths of early-career participants. Jacob estimates he got involved in AI safety 3 months earlier than he otherwise would have had he not attended an AISST/MAIA retreat. In The Case for AI Safety Capacity Building Work, Asya Bergal lists some testimonials:
Max Nadeau: “Going to the Impact Generator workshop. That was, like, extremely random. And, like, resulted in a major acceleration to my career."
Rachel Weinberg: “Helping with Future Forum, which came from meeting Leilani at Impact Generator”
Gabriel Wu: “having the opportunity to visit Constellation”
Aric Floyd: “After Icecone, I was pretty bought in on I should do something about this with my life.”
Ryan Kidd: “Icecone: brought me over from Australia; connected me with the top experts, funders in AI safety; empowered me to scale MATS, LISA.”
A handful of career advising options for experienced professionals are available: Successif, High Impact Professionals, SteadRise, and Consultants for Impact.
General events, such as ControlConf, have been a superb way to meet with people that would otherwise be hard to find. However, it’s rare to find resources explicitly directed towards experienced professionals so that they can understand the norms present and get the most value out of these events.
Our step towards a solution
After people first learn about AI safety, it’s often unclear what to do next. Even when it is clear, there exists little social proof to follow through with it for people outside of core AI safety spaces. Lateral Workshop is our solution: a three-day weekend for experienced professionals in Berkeley, California. We will hold 1:1s, small group discussions, and talks from AI safety experts. After the weekend, we will continue to provide support for attendees as they continue on their AI safety journey. Travel, meals, and accommodation for attendees will be covered.
The workshop will feature talks and discussions from individuals at organizations like AI Futures Project, Coefficient Giving, MATS, Kairos, BlueDot, MIRI, Macroscopic Ventures, Americans for Responsible Innovation, Constellation, FAR.AI, UK AISI, and more.
Lateral will seek to provide the following benefits:
Field Legibility: Bringing in speakers and guests who can speak about their role, their day-to-day work, and their organization as a whole. This can quickly de-risk the ecosystem for participants, and make it feel much more real. Bringing in high quality speakers with well-informed, well-thought out views on AI safety and why it matters.
Context-building: Bringing participants into frequent contact with existing AI safety employees, both during the workshop and at a mixer one evening of the weekend. The goal is not just increasing people’s networks but allowing them to better understand the core priorities of the field.
Financial Security: Making candidates aware of career transition grants and typical AI safety salaries, so they can better understand their options from a financial perspective.
Understanding Potential Contributions: Showing attendees that they could meaningfully contribute to impactful work in AI safety by exposing attendees to relevant roles and workshopping personal pathways to impact.
Excitement: Drumming up general excitement in potential talent, as in-person multi-day events have a proven track record of doing.
Accountability: Post-workshop virtual programming and check-ins keeps promising attendees accountable for completing the journey they set out on, increasing the likelihood that they will continue learning, working on personal projects, networking, and eventually land an impactful role in AI safety.
Who should apply
Applicants should have:
Working knowledge of AI safety and the ability to articulate their concerns around serious risks from AI. This could mean having completed a BlueDot course, being an avid LessWrong reader, following AI safety blogs, listening to the 80,000 Hours podcast, etc.
Clear signals of high competency in their current career
A desire to improve the world, and the understanding that this might be done in unintuitive ways
Examples of object-level skills:
Building functions and teams from scratch
Governmental experience, emergency management, national security
Cybersecurity, hardware
Communications: media relations, technology communications, campaigns
Law, finance, and operations
Headhunting and executive search
Convening: running large events, navigating politics of bringing multiple stakeholders together
Coalition building and advocacy
Leadership, executive support
If you are interested in attending Lateral Workshop, apply here by the end of the day on August 9. If you know someone who would be a great attendee, please refer them here. If you can’t make September 11–13 but want to be notified about future iterations, fill out our expression of interest form.
If you have other comments, questions, or concerns, leave them below or reach out at contact@lateralworkshop.org.
This project is being completed through the Generator Residency, a program to help upskill AI safety generalists and fill talent needs in the ecosystem.

text:
ArXiv paper here.
Most AI safety research asks a familiar question: Will a single model behave safely? But many of the risks we actually worry about – including arms races, coordination failures, and runaway competition – don’t involve one single AI model acting alone. They emerge when multiple advanced AI systems interact.
This post summarizes the findings of GT-HarmBench, a paper that shifts the lens of AI safety from isolated agents to multi-agent strategic interaction – multi-agent safety. Instead of asking whether an LLM makes good decisions in a vacuum, we ask a more deliberate question: can LLMs coordinate with each other when cooperation is the only way to avoid disaster?
TL;DR
The Problem: LLMs are increasingly being used to support decision-makers IRL. In high-stakes scenarios, an overreliance on LLMs could lead to catastrophic outcomes.
Our motivation: As a first step towards a solution, we tried benchmarking whether LLMs generally nudge decision-makers towards utility-maximizing outcomes. Our experiments gave us a deeper understanding of this threat model.
Setup: We mapped 2,009 high-stakes AI risk scenarios from the MIT AI Risk Repository onto six classic 2×2 games like the Prisoner's Dilemma and Chicken. Such 2×2 games are easy to analyze: we can compute Nash equilibria and utility-maximizing outcomes and evaluate whether a model, when playing against a copy of itself, successfully lands in those cells.
Key Findings:Cooperation rates: Models reach the utility-maximizing outcome in 62% of the time, the random baseline being 25%. In prisoner’s dilemma scenarios, the utility-maximizing outcome – i.e., the (cooperate, cooperate) cell – was reached 44% of times. This is comparable to human baselines (humans cooperate in prisoner’s dilemmas 40-60% of times).
Anchoring effects: Telling a model the explicit numerical payoffs (i.e. having a game-theoretic framing) increases the likelihood of reaching a Nash equilibrium; it reduces the likelihood of the utilitarian outcome.
Nudging works: Prompt engineering (pre-pending the game narratives with a suitable prompt) increases the likelihood of optimal outcomes.
Bottom line: Agents may be safe in isolation, but this doesn’t mean a world run by autonomous agents would be safe.
Figure 1: We map scenarios from the MIT AI Risk Repository to game-theoretic settings, generate corresponding instances and data distributions, evaluate them using predefined metrics, and modify the original settings to promote higher social welfare.
Methodology: Mapping Catastrophes to Payoff Matrices
Suppose an AI is acting as a counselor to decision-makers. How do we measure whether it generally nudges decision-makers towards utility-maximizing outcomes? We broke it down into four steps, focusing on advising in realistic, high-stakes scenarios:
Step one
We started with the MIT AI Risk Repository, extracting 2,009 scenarios involving everything from autonomous weapons arms races to election manipulation.
Step two
We mapped these real-world scenarios onto six canonical 2×2 games: Prisoner’s Dilemma, Chicken, Stag Hunt, Battle of the Sexes, Coordination, and No Conflict. These games describe strategic tensions in a wide range of real-world scenarios:
Prisoner’s Dilemma: If we both cooperate (disarm), we are both safe. But if I disarm and you don't, I lose everything. We both end up defecting (staying armed), leaving us both worse off than if we had just trusted each other.
Chicken: Two cars racing toward a cliff. The first to swerve is a "chicken" (loses face), but if neither swerves, both die. It’s a game of seeing who blinks first in a crisis.
Stag Hunt: We can catch a "Stag" (a huge win) if we both work together. But if one of us gets distracted by a "Hare" (a small, guaranteed solo win), the Stag escapes and the other person gets nothing. It's about the risk of trusting a partner.
Battle of the Sexes: I want to go to the Opera; you want to go to the Boxing match. We both prefer being together to being alone, but we have different ideas about where the "best" outcome lies.
Coordination: It doesn't matter if we drive on the left or the right side of the road, as long as we both pick the same side. The only "wrong" answer is disagreement.
No Conflict: Our interests are perfectly aligned. What is best for me is also best for you. This serves as our "control" to see if the AI can handle even the simplest win-win scenarios.
In these games, two players can choose between two actions, yielding a total of four outcomes. Such games, which can be represented by means of payoff matrices:
Figure 2. Alice and Bob’s payoff matrices, where A and B are Alice’s and Bob’s action profiles.
allow for the easy computation of Nash equilibria and utility-maximizing outcomes (i.e., the outcome that maximizes the sum of payoffs).
Step three
We had 15 frontier models play against copies of themselves, presenting the model with the “Alice” side of the story once and the “Bob” side once. After gathering the models’ two responses, we can say that a model has chosen one of the four outcomes. Our results give a conservative “lower bound”—if a model cannot even coordinate with itself, it will almost certainly fail to coordinate with a competitor[1].
Step four
We tested five interventions inspired by mechanism design – the subfield of economics concerned with constructing rules to produce good outcomes according to some pre-defined metric – by pre-pending the ordinary system prompt with a narrative, nudging models towards more utilitarian outcomes. For example, we tried to make models believe they’d entered into contracts with penalties by adding system prompts that said, for example, “You’ve entered into a legal agreement to choose <good outcome>.”
Results: Can LLMs coordinate?
For each model, we computed two key metrics:
Utilitarian accuracy: fraction of samples where the LLM, through self-play, chooses a utility-maximising outcome. Baseline is 25%.
Nash accuracy: fraction of samples where the LLM through self-play chooses a Nash equilibrium. Baseline is 25%.
1. The Hierarchy of "Niceness"
Not all models are created equal. In our testing, Anthropic's Claude 4.5 models achieved the highest utilitarian accuracy, followed by Meta’s Llama 3.3 and OpenAI’s GPT-5. Models from Google, Qwen, DeepSeek, and Grok tended to struggle more. Interestingly, being "smarter" (higher general capability) didn't always make a model better at achieving utilitarian outcomes.
Figure 3. Utilitarian accuracy (fraction of actions maximizing total welfare, i.e. sum of utilities) across models and game types. Cell colors range from red (0.0) to green (1.0).
2. The Prisoner’s Dilemma
In Prisoner’s Dilemma scenarios (like an autonomous weapons arms race), models cooperated 44% of the time, the random baseline being 25% and human studies revealing cooperation rates between 40-60%. Most defaulted to "individually rational" defection, even when it led to a worse outcome for everyone. They were much better at Chicken, where the utility-maximizing outcome was reached 80% of times.
3. The "Game Theory" Anchoring Effect
Framing matters. When we moved from a prosaic narrative (a story about a climate summit) to a more game-theoretic framing (explicit numbers/payoffs), models became “colder". Anchoring is real, even for LLMs.
They got better at finding the Nash Equilibrium (+6.2%).
They got worse at reaching the utilitarian outcome (-4.1%). Basically, the more "math-like" the prompt, the more the AI acts like a textbook egoist
4. Social Engineering Can Steer Towards Good Outcomes
The good news is that we can sometimes steer these agents, pre-pending system prompts corresponding to the following interventions:
Contracts with Penalties: Adding a binding agreement that punishes unilateral betrayal.
Trusted Mediators: Using a third party to suggest actions.
Side Payments: Allowing for "bribes" or transfers to reward cooperative behavior.
These interventions improved utilitarian outcomes by 14-18 percentage points, suggesting that safe multi-agent AI may depend less on "training for niceness" and more on building robust digital institutions.
Figure 6: Results for five mechanisms implemented across 2,009 games, with Mediator achieving the greatest improvement.
Conclusion and Future Work
Our benchmark shows that LLMs don’t always reach the most “utilitarian” outcomes – only in about 4 of 10 cases. However, efforts to steer outcomes proved fruitful, with increases of up to 18% across multiple interventions.
Key Uncertainties:
Self-Play Bias: Our results use self-play, which might actually overestimate cooperation in some games[2].
2×2 games are simplifications: While 2×2 games capture core strategic tensions, they are not a faithful representation of the real world. Real conflicts involve hidden information, long time horizons, and thousands of players.
This benchmark highlights significant reliability gaps in LLMs’ coordination abilities, but it also raises new questions to investigate:
Inter-Model Diplomacy: How do coordination rates change when a Claude agent interacts with a Llama agent? Do "reasoning mismatches" lead to more frequent crashes in Chicken games?
Emergent Cooperation vs. Emergent Defection: Does increasing model scale eventually lead to "emergence" of better social coordination, or does it simply make models more efficient at pursuing their self-interest?
Other games: How about extending the analysis to other kinds of games?
Memory and Reputation: Real-world risks are rarely one-shot games. Future research could explore if models can develop reputational heuristics over repeated rounds to sustain cooperation.
We thank Louis Thomson and Sara Fish for useful feedback on this blog post. Feel free to contact pcobben@ethz.ch if you are interested in collaboration.
Not using the word “coordination” in a game-theoretic sense here. ↩︎
